THE HUMAN ATLASES · DEEP DIVE

The branching human family

The oldest possible members of the human lineage are millions of years older than Lucy. Later, Australopithecus and Paranthropus overlapped with early Homo, and several populations of Homo shared parts of Eurasia. Fossils document this diversity. DNA from later groups also shows where branches met again.

A selected fossil and molecular record from Africa and Eurasia, updated through November 2026. Early occurrence ages and first modern discoveries describe different events. For small fossil samples, named localities are grouped into regional map markers where appropriate.

What a first occurrence measures

Hominins include living humans and extinct species more closely related to us than to chimpanzees and bonobos. Near the split, researchers compare such clues as tooth form, the base of the skull and anatomy related to bipedal movement. An isolated bone or tooth can fit more than one evolutionary interpretation. [62] [63] [64]

A fossil’s age establishes a known occurrence in a particular region. The lineage may have originated earlier or elsewhere. A type specimen anchors a scientific name, and an older find assigned to that name can change the first occurrence. Ma means million years ago and ka means thousand years ago. [62] [32]

Late Miocene and early Pliocene candidates

Toros-Menalla, the Tugen Hills and the Middle Awash preserve different parts of the earliest fossil record. The 2026 study of limb fragments from Chad strengthens a bipedal interpretation for Sahelanthropus, while the fragmentary remains and disagreements over their anatomy leave its place near the hominin split open. [1] [63] [64] [62]

Australopithecus and Paranthropus

The Ethiopian fossils suggest possible overlap between late Australopithecus anamensis and early Australopithecus afarensis. The latter coexisted in the broader East African region with forms given other names, among them Australopithecus deyiremeda and Kenyanthropus platyops. Comparisons of teeth and feet help assess how these populations differed in diet and locomotion. [12] [15] [13] [18]

Paranthropus is the name commonly used for several hominins with specialized chewing anatomy. At Nyayanga, two teeth place the genus early on the Homa Peninsula. Their association with Oldowan artifacts leaves open whether Paranthropus, another hominin or more than one group used the stone technology there. [32] [24]

Early Homo in Africa and Eurasia

A fragmentary lower jaw from Ledi-Geraru is the oldest widely cited fossil assigned to Homo. At different localities in the same research area, fossils document Homo around 2.78 and 2.59 Ma and an unnamed Australopithecus around 2.63 Ma. Together with Paranthropus at Mille-Logya around 2.6 Ma, the finds place several lineages in the Afar during this interval. [25] [34] [30] [28] [78] [77]

Shangchen and Dmanisi illustrate why fossil dates and activity dates deserve separate entries. Shangchen’s older stone horizons have no identified makers. The oldest tools at Dmanisi predate the main skeleton-bearing layer there, which contains multiple individuals whose variation has invited different species names. [68] [37] [38]

Middle and Late Pleistocene diversity

Later fossils are still difficult to place in a single tree. The name Homo heidelbergensis has been applied narrowly to specimens resembling the Mauer mandible or more broadly to several Middle Pleistocene populations. Other fossils reveal local branches, such as the small-bodied hominins on Flores and the cave finds on Luzon. [70] [42] [43] [61]

Denisovans and the evidence for contact

Denisovans are a late branch of the human family, first identified through DNA from Denisova Cave. The oldest well-contextualized Denisovan fossils there date to about 200 ka, and cave sediment preserves their mitochondrial DNA in older deposits. Lucy lived about 3.2 Ma and the earliest candidate hominins date to around 7 Ma. The known age of a fossil or sediment sample also differs from the time its lineage separated from another. [49] [72] [50] [19] [1]

Denisovans and Neanderthals are closely related lineages. A bone fragment at Denisova Cave yielded the genome of a girl with a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Denisovan-derived DNA in some living people records other encounters, including with ancestors of present-day populations in Oceania. The molecular lineage spans fossils assigned different species names, including the Harbin cranium originally named Homo longi. Proposed names and the range of fossils they cover remain debated. [72] [73] [55] [51]

What genetic and molecular evidence can establish

Ancient DNA is a physical trace from a particular specimen, but turning it into a population history requires comparison and modelling. Researchers test contamination, fragment damage and consistency across extracts, then compare patterns across many sites in the genome. A resemblance at one position is weaker evidence than a consistent genome-wide pattern. [73] [85]

The categories below answer different questions. A protein-based lineage assignment, a maternal genealogy and a genome-wide admixture estimate should never be presented as interchangeable measurements. [39] [41]

EvidenceWhat it can showWhat it cannot show aloneSources
Nuclear DNAMany inherited regions from both parents can identify close kinship, population affinities and introgressed segments.Sequenced individuals remain a small sample; estimated contact dates depend on generation lengths, recombination and demographic assumptions.[73] [85]
Mitochondrial DNAA largely maternally inherited genealogy, often recoverable when nuclear DNA is scarce.One maternal line is not the whole family tree. Sima nuclear DNA is Neanderthal-related although its mitochondrial affinity is Denisovan-related.[41]
Ancient proteinsSurviving amino-acid variants can place fossils near a lineage beyond the usual DNA preservation window.A small set of proteins cannot substitute for a whole genome or normally measure a person’s genome-wide admixture fraction.[39]
Fossil shape and archaeological contextAnatomical comparisons, dating and geographic presence; tools document behavior.A mosaic of traits is not by itself proof of interbreeding, and tools do not necessarily identify their makers.[70] [61]

Interbreeding: a child, recent ancestors and older gene flow

Denisova 11 is unusually direct evidence. Slon and colleagues (2018) found the genome-wide pattern expected for a first-generation daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father. Her father also carried older Neanderthal ancestry. This establishes parentage for one individual; it does not reveal where her parents met or whether she later had children. [73]

Oase 1 from Romania supplies a different kind of evidence. Fu and colleagues (2015) inferred a Neanderthal ancestor roughly four to six generations back from very long inherited segments. Their estimate of about 6–9% Neanderthal ancestry describes this approximately 42–37-thousand-year-old individual, not all early Europeans. [84]

For older contact, recombination breaks inherited segments into shorter pieces across generations. Iasi and colleagues (2024) modelled most shared Neanderthal gene flow in their samples within an extended interval about 50.5–43.5 thousand years ago. Sümer and colleagues, published online in 2024, obtained approximately 49–45 thousand years from early European genomes. Different models and samples give related estimates, not an exact date for every encounter. [85] [86]

Introgressed DNA persisting in later populations demonstrates that at least some mixed descendants reproduced. It does not mean every pairing was fertile or that the lineages had no barriers to gene flow. Species names remain classifications; limited interbreeding and long-term genetic differentiation can coexist. [73] [70]

Geographic differences in inherited ancestry

The comparisons below refer to sampled people and published analyses. They are not fixed racial percentages or properties of everyone living in a region. Later migration, population mixing, selection and the choice of reference genomes change both the distribution of ancestry and its estimated amount. Modern sample locations also do not locate prehistoric encounters. [90] [87] [85]

Sampled region or populationPublished patternHow to read the comparisonSources
Europe and western EurasiaIasi et al. (2024) summarize roughly 1–2% Neanderthal ancestry for most present-day people with ancestry outside Africa.Individual histories vary; early people such as Oase had much higher recent contributions and are not an average for the region.[85] [84]
East AsiaNeanderthal ancestry is widespread; studies also detect Denisovan-derived segments with more than one affinity to the Altai genome.Some methods estimate more Neanderthal sequence than in European samples. The size of that difference depends on reference choice and demographic modelling.[87] [90]

Tibetan PlateauA Denisovan-like EPAS1 haplotype contributed to high-altitude adaptation in the 2014 study.A selected locus can be common without a similarly high genome-wide ancestry fraction; the fossil and admixture histories are separate questions.[93]
Sampled African populations: Neanderthal-related segmentsChen et al. (2020) detected appreciable apparent Neanderthal sequence in their African samples and modelled an important role for back-migration.Signals differ across samples. Some sequence sharing also reflects older human-to-Neanderthal gene flow, so a matching segment is not automatically a direct Neanderthal-to-African event.[90]
Western, eastern and southern African population historiesDurvasula and Sankararaman (2020) inferred an unsampled archaic contribution in West African data; Ragsdale et al. (2023) fit deep structure with prolonged gene flow across African ancestral populations.These are competing demographic explanations, not a confirmed fossil species assignment or one percentage for Africa.[92] [91]

Africa: back-migration and unresolved deep ancestry

Africa has its own complex population history. Chen and colleagues (2020) used a method that does not require a supposedly unadmixed modern African reference. Their results support movement back into Africa by people whose ancestors had acquired Neanderthal ancestry in Eurasia. They also show that older gene flow from early modern humans into Neanderthals can produce sequence sharing. Neither process requires Neanderthals themselves to have lived at the location of a present-day African sample. [90]

An additional question concerns deep ancestry without a matching ancient genome. Durvasula and Sankararaman (2020) inferred gene flow from an unsampled divergent population in four West African datasets. Their model-dependent ancestry estimates had a broad 2–19% range across analyses. That range is not a measured universal African fraction, and the study cannot identify the source as H. naledi, H. erectus or another named fossil species. [92]

Ragsdale and colleagues (2023) tested a wider set of histories, including new Nama genomes alongside eastern and western African comparisons. Models with weakly differentiated ancestral populations exchanging genes for long periods explained signals previously attributed to a sharply separated archaic source. This does not prove that all archaic contact was absent; it shows that a genetic pattern can have more than one plausible demographic explanation. [91]

Sampling, percentages and the missing branches

Ancient genomes are unevenly preserved and sampled. A sequenced Altai Denisovan is a reference individual, not a complete representation of Denisovan diversity. Browning et al. (2018) and Jacobs et al. (2019) found patterns inconsistent with a single uniform Denisovan source. Dates, number of contacts and inferred source relationships can change when new genomes are added. [87] [88]

Analyses also differ in which sites they measure. Iasi et al. (2024) found that a commonly used ancient-DNA capture panel contained too few archaic-informative sites for their intended ancestry analysis and selected suitable genome or capture datasets. A reported percentage therefore needs its method and comparison samples, not just a population label. [85]

Proteins extend the molecular record: Homo antecessor enamel gives information much older than most hominin DNA. But limited protein variation can leave relationships unresolved. For many named fossil lineages, including the early australopiths and the island taxa, we lack genomes that could directly test particular interbreeding claims. No recovered DNA is not evidence that no contact occurred; equally, possible contact is not demonstrated gene flow. [39] [60] [61] [70]

Genome-wide ancestry and particular inherited variants also behave differently. Selection can favor an advantageous variant such as the Denisovan-like EPAS1 haplotype while other introgressed regions are lost. A variant’s present frequency does not measure the number of ancient encounters or a person’s overall ancestry. [93] [85]

What became of the other lineages?

A lineage can disappear as a distinct population while some of its ancestry continues in another. Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA in later humans demonstrates partial genetic survival. It does not show that every local group was absorbed, identify a single cause of disappearance, or establish that an ancient individual with no detected contribution to sampled people had no descendants at all. [72] [84] [86]

The final known fossil is a minimum record of how late a lineage existed, not the date its last member died. The dated Ngandong bone bed records H. erectus at about 117–108 thousand years ago. Revised Liang Bua dates place H. floresiensis bones around 100–60 thousand years ago; whether the lineage survived later remains open. [94] [60]

Denisovan history also differs by place. The 2025 Denisova Cave synthesis records changes in maternal lineages and late local evidence around 55 thousand years ago, while the Baishiya rib occurs in a layer dated about 48–32 thousand years ago. Neither site supplies a global extinction date. Naledi and luzonensis have still more limited geographic records; their disappearance and any genetic legacy remain unresolved. [49] [54] [46] [61]

For the much earlier branches, fossils document diversity, overlap and anatomical change, while their exact relationships remain debated. A chronological sequence on this map is not a claim that each named species transformed into the next. Missing markers reflect the selected evidence and preservation record, not an empty continent. [70] [39]

  • Laetoli footprint trails — Footprints in volcanic ash document upright walking about 3.66 million years ago.
  • Nyayanga — Early Oldowan artifacts, processed animal bones and Paranthropus teeth occur on Kenya’s Homa Peninsula.
  • Bokol Dora 1, Ledi-Geraru — Early Oldowan flaking in Ethiopia’s Afar dates to about 2.61–2.58 million years ago.
  • Gona Oldowan localities — Several Afar localities preserve some of the best studied Oldowan tools from around 2.6 million years ago.
  • Shangchen, Chinese Loess Plateau — Tool-bearing layers in Shaanxi document early activity outside Africa from about 2.12 million years ago.
